title: John Finley, the Trader Who Put Kentucky on Boone’s Map
summary: Fur trader John Finley reached Kentucky years before Daniel Boone, then described the country to Boone and guided him through the Cumberland Gap in 1769.
bodyMarkdown:
John Finley, also spelled Findley (c. 1724 – c. 1783), was a fur trader who traveled into Kentucky years before Daniel Boone. He is best known for describing the country to Boone and for guiding him through the Cumberland Gap in 1769. Finley's knowledge came from Native towns and trade routes, not from empty wilderness.

## A trader on the Warrior's Path

Little is known of Finley's early life. An account of [John Finley](https://grokipedia.com/page/john_finley_%28frontiersman%29) says he likely came from Pennsylvania or Virginia, and that by the early 1750s he was trading in Native territory. In 1752 he is believed to have reached Eskippakithiki, a Shawnee village in present Clark County. It was possibly the first documented European-American trading expedition into central Kentucky.

Eskippakithiki was a real town with a long history. A Kentucky Historical Society marker in Clark County calls it the last Indian town in Kentucky and says Finley had a store there in 1752. The marker gives the town's span as about 1715 to 1754.

Other sources give different dates. It was founded around [1718](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/596), and an account of [Eskippakithiki](https://grokipedia.com/page/eskippakithiki) agrees on about 1718 but says it was abandoned in 1754–55. It was a [palisaded town of about 200 families](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/596). One account gives a different translation of the name.

## The end of the town

A band of Ottawa [attacked Eskippakithiki about 1753](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/596), which may have prompted its abandonment soon after. That episode is told in [The Odawa raid at Eskippakithiki](/stories/odawa-raid-at-eskippakithiki-1753/). Historians believe the town's people eventually joined other Shawnee in southern Ohio.

## Finley and Boone

Finley and Boone reportedly met during the French and Indian War. Finley told Boone about the fertile land beyond the Cumberland Gap, drawn from his own trading in Kentucky, and this stirred Boone's interest.

In 1769 the two met again in North Carolina. Boone [set out](https://grokipedia.com/page/Daniel_Boone) on May 1, 1769, with John Findley as guide, John Stewart and three others, and crossed the gap in late May or early June. The Clark County marker says Boone first viewed the area on June 7, 1769. For the gap itself, see [Thomas Walker and Cumberland Gap](/stories/thomas-walker-and-cumberland-gap/).

## Later years

After the 1769 expedition Finley largely drops out of the record. Some sources suggest he kept trading in the west, but his activities after the 1770s are mostly undocumented. He is believed to have died by 1783.

Historians credit Finley with a key role in opening Kentucky to Anglo-American settlement. His firsthand knowledge of Native trade routes and geography helped Boone and the settlers who followed.

## Kentucky today

A state marker in Clark County recalls Eskippakithiki and its Shawnee residents. It also names Finley's 1752 store and Boone's 1769 visit.
